title: Delivering Data When Packets Get Lost

sections.title: A packet vanishes
sections.narration: A packet disappears, and the sender hears nothing. Was the message lost, or just the reply? That uncertainty is enough to cause duplicates, endless waiting, or missing data. Let's build a way out.
bullets: How can it know what arrived?
sections.takeaway: Reliability requires feedback and carefully tracked state.

sections.title: Read the timeline
sections.narration: Read this picture as a timeline. The sender is on the left, the receiver on the right, and time moves downward. Sloping arrows cross the distance; returning arrows carry acknowledgments, small messages that report progress.
sections.takeaway: A timeline separates transmission, arrival, and acknowledgment events.

sections.title: Send one, then wait
sections.narration: Start with the simplest rule: send one packet, keep a copy, and wait for confirmation before sending another. This is stop-and-wait. Keeping the copy gives the sender something to use if the attempt fails.
sections.takeaway: Stop-and-wait permits one unacknowledged packet at a time.

sections.title: Choose an ACK convention
sections.narration: We need one precise convention. An ACK names the next packet expected. ACK one confirms packet zero; ACK four confirms zero through three. That number points to the first missing position in the ordered sequence.
bullets: ACK n means next expected n
sections.takeaway: Every ACK number here identifies the next packet expected.

sections.title: Notice the idle gap
sections.narration: Notice the empty space after transmission. The packet is still travelling, and its acknowledgment must travel back. The sender could have more data ready, yet our rule leaves it idle until that round trip finishes.
sections.takeaway: Long feedback delay can leave a fast link mostly idle.

sections.title: Separate two kinds of time
sections.narration: Two delays explain this gap. Transmission time measures putting the bits onto the link; propagation time measures their travel. A faster transmitter reduces one delay without making the signal itself cross the distance instantly.
sections.takeaway: Transmission time and propagation delay measure different things.

sections.title: Calculate stop-and-wait use
sections.narration: Here, transmission takes one millisecond and round-trip propagation takes twenty. Ignoring other overhead, only one millisecond in twenty-one is spent sending useful data: about four point eight percent. The waiting dominates the work.
sections.takeaway: With negligible ACK cost, utilization is 1 divided by 21, about 4.8 percent.

sections.title: Lose the data packet
sections.narration: Now lose the packet. No acknowledgment returns, but silence doesn't reveal the cause. The data might be missing, its acknowledgment might be missing, or either could simply be late. Waiting forever cannot resolve that uncertainty.
bullets: No new ACK can confirm it
sections.takeaway: A missing acknowledgment leaves the sender uncertain.

sections.title: Expire a timer
sections.narration: A timer gives the sender a decision point. When enough time passes without confirmation, recovery begins. Notice what it hasn't established: a timeout is a reason to retry, not proof that the original packet vanished.
sections.takeaway: A timeout detects missing confirmation, not certain packet loss.

sections.title: Retransmit the saved copy
sections.narration: The saved copy is sent again with the same sequence number. This attempt reaches the receiver, and ACK one returns. With progress confirmed, the sender can release that copy and prepare the next packet.
sections.takeaway: Retransmission retries the same logical packet.

sections.title: Lose the acknowledgment instead
sections.narration: Change just one event: deliver the data, but lose its acknowledgment. The sender sees the same silence and retries. Now a perfectly reasonable recovery creates a second arrival. How can the receiver avoid delivering the contents twice?
sections.takeaway: The sender may retry data that the receiver already has.

sections.title: Recognize the duplicate
sections.narration: The sequence number answers that question. The receiver expects one, so another zero is a duplicate. It repeats ACK one without delivering the data again. Repeating transmission doesn't have to mean repeating delivery to the application.
sections.takeaway: Sequence state distinguishes a duplicate from new data.

sections.title: Why alternating bits can work
sections.narration: For basic stop-and-wait, alternating zero and one can distinguish successive packets under suitable initialization and old-duplicate assumptions. Our larger numbers make the examples easier to track, but sequence information needn't always be a large counter.
sections.takeaway: A small sequence space requires careful assumptions about delayed duplicates.

sections.title: Choose a sensible timeout
sections.narration: Set the timer too short and late packets trigger unnecessary retries. Set it too long and actual losses cause long stalls. This delayed acknowledgment exposes the balance. Real protocols can estimate delays and adapt their timers.
sections.takeaway: A timer trades quick recovery against unnecessary retransmission.

sections.title: Allow four packets in flight
sections.narration: Can we use the waiting time? Allow four unconfirmed packets instead of one. The sending window limits how much data may be outstanding. It changes the sender's permission to proceed, without adding another physical link.
sections.takeaway: A sender window permits several packets before confirmation.

sections.title: Fill the pipeline
sections.narration: Now zero, one, two, and three follow each other into the network. Earlier packets travel while later ones leave, and acknowledgments return behind them. The same link carries more useful work because we stopped waiting after every packet.
sections.takeaway: Pipelining overlaps useful transmission with feedback travel.

sections.title: Use cumulative acknowledgments
sections.narration: ACK three confirms the complete run through packet two. That's cumulative acknowledgment: one reply can report progress across several packets. The boundary can advance only through consecutive received data, leaving a gap as the stopping point.
bullets: An earlier missing ACK may be covered
sections.takeaway: Cumulative ACKs confirm a contiguous prefix of received data.

sections.title: Slide the sending window
sections.narration: In this separate example, ACK two confirms zero and one. The window moves forward two positions, allowing new packets at its far edge. Follow the boundary: the allowed range moves, while its size stays four.
sections.takeaway: Acknowledgments advance the window and permit new transmissions.

sections.title: Go-Back-N: lose packet 1
sections.narration: Now lose packet one after sending zero through three. Zero arrives, so the receiver asks for one. We pause new sends here to isolate the problem: the sender still lacks confirmation for one, two, and three.
sections.takeaway: A gap prevents contiguous in-order acceptance in this Go-Back-N model.

sections.title: Discard later arrivals
sections.narration: Our basic Go-Back-N receiver discards two and three because one is missing. Each later arrival prompts ACK one again. Those packets reached the destination, but this protocol hasn't accepted them into the ordered sequence.
sections.takeaway: A basic Go-Back-N receiver discards out-of-order packets.

sections.title: Retransmit from the gap
sections.narration: When packet one's timer expires, the sender retries one, two, and three. Zero remains confirmed. This explains Go-Back-N's extra work after a loss: recovery repeats the outstanding sequence starting at the gap.
sections.takeaway: Go-Back-N retransmits outstanding packets starting at the oldest unconfirmed one.

sections.title: Accept the repaired sequence
sections.narration: The repeated packets now arrive in order. ACK four advances the boundary past three, releasing the saved copies. The number still means the next packet wanted. Our convention stays consistent through both failure and recovery.
sections.takeaway: Once the gap is repaired, in-order acceptance and window movement resume.

sections.title: Compare the mechanisms carefully
sections.narration: Compare windows of one, four, and twenty-one. More outstanding packets can fill the waiting time, but can't exceed the link's capacity. TCP uses related ideas with byte numbers and additional mechanisms beyond this simplified packet model.
sections.takeaway: Modern TCP is related to ARQ ideas but is not this exact frame protocol.

sections.title: Reconstruct reliability yourself
sections.narration: Reliability emerged from a few pieces working together: confirmations, saved copies, timers, sequence numbers, and a moving window. Each solves a different failure. Together, they let communication recover when the path can eventually carry data.
sections.takeaway: Recovery needs feedback and state; permanent link failure can still stop delivery.
